title: Portrait and Winter
premise: Quentin Winterbourne takes a teaching post at Marrow Fen Academy, where students vanish from class rosters one by one and the staff's official records rewrite themselves overnight. He discovers the school's founder, in 1974, bound a dying child's identity into a portrait to preserve his own power, and every winter the portrait 'collects' new faces to stay alive. When Quentin's own sleep recordings reveal a second voice—his, but older, answering questions he never asked—he realizes he was chosen before he ever arrived. To end it, he must return what was taken: give the stolen child back her name, her face, and her winter, even if it means surrendering his own.
about_author: Cyrus Underhill is the pen name of a former boarding-school caretaker who spent eleven winters on the grounds of a shuttered New England academy. His fiction draws on institutional archives, oral histories of vanished students, and a personal refusal to explain away what he saw in the north stairwell.

chapters.title: The Roster That Breathes
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Arriving at Marrow Fen Academy mid-winter term, Quentin notices the class roster lists thirty-one students for a room of twenty-eight desks. The headmaster, Voss, laughs it off as a printing error. Emotional beat: uneasy curiosity masked by professional detachment; Quentin resolves to be the invisible teacher who asks nothing.

chapters.title: Attendance Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. During roll call, three names receive answers from empty air—and the other students write them down without being told. A girl named Ilsa Corrigan warns him not to mark anyone absent. Emotional beat: first crack in his skepticism; the ritual normalcy of the class frightens him more than any ghost could.

chapters.title: What the Frost Draws on Glass
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Frost patterns appear on his classroom windows spelling fragments of names no current student bears. In the archive basement he finds a 1974 yearbook with one face scratched out. Emotional beat: dread deepening into obsession; he begins keeping his own private ledger.

chapters.title: The Sleep Recordings
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Insomniac, Quentin sets a recorder by his bed. Playback reveals a second voice—dry, patient, unmistakably his own timbre—answering questions in a language that predates the school. Emotional beat: violation; the last private room in his mind has been entered.

chapters.title: Ilsa Knows the Words
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Through Ilsa's eyes we learn the students' side: they are taught the second voice's vocabulary in dreams, and each winter one of them is 'promoted' into the portrait. She recognizes Quentin's voice from her own recordings. Emotional beat: terrified solidarity; she decides to trust the new teacher.

chapters.title: Portrait of a Founder
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. The founder's oil portrait in the great hall has fresh paint over old paint—decades of retouching, each layer a slightly different face. Voss catches him studying it and, for the first time, stops smiling. Emotional beat: the mask slips; Quentin understands the administration is complicit, not ignorant.

chapters.title: The Missing-Class Problem
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. A student, Tomas, vanishes between second period and lunch. Every record now shows Tomas never enrolled; only Quentin's handwritten notes remember him. Emotional beat: gaslit grief and rage—the corruption isn't supernatural alone; people choose to forget.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ilsa leads Quentin to the sealed east wing, where a child's bedroom sits preserved: Edith Marrow, the founder's daughter, who died in the winter of '74 while her father learned to bind souls into pigment. Emotional beat: pity curdling into horror; the portrait is wearing a dead girl's patience.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Speaks Plainly
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. The recording voice finally addresses Quentin directly through the tape: it is Edith, or what remains of her, and she has been riding his sleep since he signed his contract. She tells him he was hired because his face fits an empty frame. Emotional beat: vertigo; his invisibility was always someone else's plan.

chapters.title: Faculty Meeting at Midnight
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Quentin confronts Voss and the senior staff. They confess the arrangement: the portrait grants the school its uncanny funding and reputation in exchange for a face each winter. They believe they are custodians, not murderers. Emotional beat: moral horror of respectable men; power corrupting into liturgy.

chapters.title: Frost Writes Its Pattern
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. The frost on every window in the school completes a single image overnight: Quentin's profile inside an oval frame. Students begin avoiding his eye contact, as if looking too long might finish the work. Emotional beat: doom made visible; Ilsa refuses to accept the pattern as final.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Taken Names
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. In the archive, Quentin reconstructs fifty years of victims from payroll gaps and unclaimed belongings—forty-nine names, each erased from every record except his own handwriting. Emotional beat: grim purpose; memory itself becomes an act of resistance.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ilsa deciphers Edith's dream-language: what the founder stole wasn't just Edith's life but her true name, written once on a card and burned into the canvas's backing. Without it, Edith can only take; with it, she could let go. Emotional beat: hope with a terrible price attached.

chapters.title: The Bargain Offered
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. The portrait speaks to Quentin directly, offering him Voss's place: immortality of a kind, the school preserved forever, his doubts dissolved. It shows him his mother's face among the painted layers. Emotional beat: temptation; the corruption theme turns inward as Quentin feels how easy surrender would be.

chapters.title: Refusal in the Great Hall
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Before the assembled faculty, Quentin refuses aloud and burns his copy of the contract. The temperature drops; the frost climbs the walls; Voss orders him confined to quarters 'for his protection.' Emotional beat: defiant clarity purchased at the cost of safety.

chapters.title: The Long Night of the Recording
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Locked in, Quentin sleeps, and Edith uses his body's hours to show him the full memory of 1974: her father's brush, her drowning breath, the card with her name pressed wet against canvas. Ilsa smuggles the tapes out through the boiler tunnels. Emotional beat: witness as salvation; suffering shared is suffering halved.

chapters.title: Allies Among the Erased
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ilsa gathers the students who still remember Tomas, plus the night janitor whose brother vanished in 1989. Together they map the portrait's ritual cycle: it must claim its face before the last frost melts. Emotional beat: found family forged in shared erasure; courage becomes collective.

chapters.title: Cutting the Canvas
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Freed by the janitor's keys, Quentin reaches the portrait with a blade—but finds the backing card already half-consumed, fused with forty-nine other names. Cutting it free may release everything, including things better left bound. Emotional beat: terror at the point of no return; he cuts anyway.

chapters.title: The Unbinding
chapters.summary: POV Quentin and Ilsa alternating. In the great hall, they speak all fifty names aloud—Edith's true name last. The portrait peels itself apart into layers of screaming paint; the stolen faces step out as brief, bright figures and dissolve. Voss tries to stop them and is taken by the thing he served. Emotional beat: cathartic climax; naming as the ultimate act of power returned.

chapters.title: Edith's Winter
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. What remains of Edith appears to Quentin one last time—not as the voice in his sleep but as a small girl seeing morning for the first time in fifty years. She gives him back the hours she borrowed and walks out into the snow, leaving small footprints that simply stop. Emotional beat: grief transfigured into peace; some debts can only be paid forward.

chapters.title: The School in March
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. With Voss gone and the portrait ash, the school faces ordinary scandal: enrollment fraud, missing-person files, a headmaster's resignation letter no one remembers writing. Ilsa testifies, and the records—finally—stay rewritten in truth's direction. Emotional beat: weary, hard-won accountability; institutions can grieve if forced to.

chapters.title: Portrait and Winter
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Quentin resigns and packs his recordings, keeping only one tape: the second voice singing, wordless, on the last night. On his windowsill at home, frost forms a single small handprint and fades. He leaves the window open every winter after. Emotional beat: quiet closure; he believes now, and belief costs him nothing but warmth he gladly gives.
